newsitem.title: TURKEY: Turkish shares claw back losses on political worry.
newsitem.headline: Turkish shares claw back losses on political worry.

text.p: Turkish shares clawed back over half of a 13 percent slump in active trade on Tuesday driven by concern about the future of Turkey's Islamist-led coalition and higher-than-expected inflation, brokers and analysts said.

The IMKB National-100 index fell 5.19 percent, or 79 points, to end the day at 1,443, sharply off an intra-session low of 1,325. Trading volume rose to 28.73 trillion lira ($232 million) from 23.14 trillion on Monday morning.

Despite the late recovery, the market was over 10 percent lower in two days on political concerns that also pushed bond yields sharply higher and prompted central bank intervention to support a weaker lira.
"A situation where the government could fall at any moment put the market under considerable pressure and pulled it lower," said Mustafa Karaahmetoglu of Sayilgan Securities.

The release of February inflation data accelerated a share sell-off fuelled by a government censure motion debate and newspaper reports indicating Deputy Prime Minister Tansu Ciller's party may consider pulling out of the coalition.
However, towards the end of the afternoon session Ciller told reporters she would not abandon the government.
"After Ciller's statement there was a wave of buying. But I think there could be renewed selling tomorrow," EGS Investment's Kutay Ultan said.
The recovery was restrained by lingering doubts about the outcome of Tuesday's parliamentary debate on a censure motion brought by the leading opposition party against the government.
The share slump followed a period of market optimism about the eight-month-old government's ability to revive a flagging privatisation programme and push ahead with structural reforms.
Shares lept 65 percent in the first two months of the year on hopes that political stability would provide a basis for stabilising an economy beleaguered by annual inflation of around 80 percent.

On Tuesday, the State Institute of Statistics said February wholesale prices rose 6.2 percent on the month and an annual 78.6 percent. Consumer prices were up a monthly 5.7 percent and 77.7 percent annually.
The figures further upset market sentiment after forecasts of 4.5-5.5 percent month-on-month inflation had boosted demand for dollars, prompting Turkish central bank intervention.

The central bank sold dollars for lira in the morning to rein in the dollar's rise to 123,770 on the inflation figures. The lira closed at 123,710 from 123,480 on Monday -- a decline also reflecting underlying dollar strength.
Bond yields jumped between 7-10 points to 104-107 percent, bankers said. "The rates will go up if the government cannot reduce tension in the coming days," a private bank treasurer said.

Confidence in the government's ability to address the economy's deep-seated problems has been eroded by a warning from military leaders about the direction Turkey was taking under its first Islamist prime minister, Necmettin Erbakan.

The military-dominated National Security Council issued a set of demands last Friday aimed at reversing recent Islamist zeal partly encouraged by Erbakan's Welfare Party. The warning has cast doubt in the market about the future of the government.
